Every host call costs a flat 10 gas as in 0.7.2

stem: The excerpt is the team's Ω_W (`write`) after fix #980. A service overwrites a key that currently holds a 100-octet value with a 5,000-octet value (ω_7…ω_10 = k_O, k_Z, v_O, v_Z). Which statement matches GP 0.8.0?
options: On success ω′_7 = 5000, the length of the value just written; if a_t > a_b the value is still stored, ω′_7 = FULL, and the missing deposit is debited from the balance at the service's next accumulation

If the post-write a_t ≤ a_b the value is stored and ω′_7 = 100, the length of the value being replaced; if a_t > a_b, ω′_7 = FULL and the account is handed back unchanged (s′ = s) — the pre-fix code had already mutated the shared Go map, so the FULL write leaked (#979)

On success ω′_7 = OK (0); a_t > a_b cannot occur for an overwrite because the storage deposit (B_I per item, B_L per octet) is only charged when a key is first created, never when its value changes size
If a_t > a_b the host call exits ☇ (panic) so that the whole accumulation collapses to the checkpointed context Y; otherwise ω′_7 = 100 and the value is stored

stem: Excerpt from the team's Ω_R (`read`) after fix #938, which added the `callerServiceID == serviceID` guard (s* = ω_7, or the caller when ω_7 = 2^64−1). Accumulating service A reads a storage key of service B, which is not accumulating in this block. Which statement is correct?
options: Ω_R(ϱ, ω, μ, s, s, d) may look up any account in d but hands back only the caller's account s (mirrored into x by G); a read of B is a pure lookup that must leave B untouched — before the guard, B's key-val was evicted from the unmatched pool, B's entry vanished from the merged δ′ and the state root diverged

Reading another service's storage is not permitted by Ω_R: for s* ≠ s the call must return WHO without touching memory, so in a compliant implementation the branch that reads B's account is unreachable and the guard is merely defensive

The read must observe the posterior state being built in this block — including writes by other services accumulated in the same round — so the cached value has to be refreshed from the context on every read rather than removed from the pool

The read must be served from the lookup-anchor snapshot exactly as `historical_lookup` does, so mutating the current-state cache is only a performance concern; the guard merely avoids repeatedly decoding B's key-vals

stem: During accumulation a service executes `ecalli 9` (`machine`, a refine-only call) with ϱ = 300 gas remaining. The team's dispatcher routes ids that are not in the invocation's table to hostCallException (below, after PR #992). What does GP 0.8.0 prescribe for this situation?
options: ω′_7 = WHAT and execution continues at the next instruction regardless of the remaining gas — nothing was executed, so an unknown or unavailable host call can never by itself trigger out-of-gas (the pre-#992 behaviour)
The machine panics (☇) with no gas charged: a host-call id outside the invocation's table is treated like an invalid instruction, and the accumulation collapses to the checkpointed context Y

The default branch of F charges M_∅ = 1000 first: ϱ′ = 300 − 1000 < 0, so the invocation exits ∞ and Ψ_A collapses to the checkpointed context Y; under the 0.7.2 flat charge of 10 the same call would have continued with ω′_7 = WHAT
The `ecalli` surfaces to the caller of Ψ_A as the exit h̄ × 9: the accumulation is aborted, treated as a host-call fault, and the service's result for this block is recorded as BAD

stem: The excerpt is the team's 0.7.2 `invoke` (Ω_K): it reads a 112-octet block at ω_8, runs inner machine n = ω_7 and writes the block back. Apart from the id shift (12 → 13), which GP 0.8.0 rule is missing from it?
options: Nested host calls: an `ecalli` executed by the inner machine must be dispatched through the refine mutator F (historical_lookup, export, …) instead of stopping the inner run and reporting HOST × h to the outer service

Resumption: on a HOST exit the saved instruction counter must stay on the `ecalli` itself, so that the outer service can re-execute that instruction after servicing the call, exactly as Ψ does for a top-level page fault
Memory: the 112-octet block need only be readable, because in 0.8.0 the inner gas and the 13 registers are handed back through ω′_7…ω′_12 rather than being written back into the block

Gas: the outer machine pays g = M_K + g_R up front (∞ if ϱ < g; g_R is the inner gas read from the block) and afterwards gets the inner's unspent g_R′ back, ϱ′ = ϱ − g + g_R′; the inner machine also carries a gas-charged flag for its current basic block

stem: The excerpt is the team's `pages` (Ω_Z) acting on inner machine n over page range [p, p+c) with mode r (ω_7…ω_10 = n, p, c, r). Compared with GP 0.8.0, which statement is correct?
options: The code is correct: Ω_Z zero-fills the range for every r ∈ 0…4 and only the resulting access differs (0 → none, 1/3 → R, 2/4 → W); the GP never distinguishes an allocation from a mode change

Two semantic gaps: for r = 0 the GP zero-fills the range and makes it inaccessible (the code leaves it untouched), and for r ∈ {3, 4} the GP keeps the contents and only changes the access to R/W (the code re-allocates zeroed pages); the WHO-before-HUH ordering matches the GP

The only gap is the error code: when r > 2 and a page of the range is inaccessible the GP returns OOB (inner memory index not accessible), as `peek`/`poke` do, rather than HUH; the page mutations themselves are right
The GP validates r ∈ 0…4 and p ≥ 16 before looking up n, so an invalid request on a non-existent machine must yield HUH, whereas the code yields WHO; the page mutations themselves are right

stem: GP 0.8.0 replaces the `sbrk` instruction with the `grow_heap` host call (index 1, present in all three invocations). A program with no RO data (so a = 32, the first RW-data page) currently has c = 8 writable RW pages (h = 40) and b = 1000; it calls grow_heap with ω_7 = 50 while ϱ = 2,000. What happens?
options: ω_7 is the desired end page (index + 1 of the last writable page): g = 275 + (50 − 40)·121 = 1,485 is charged, pages [40, 50) become writable and ω′_7 = 50; with ω_7 ≤ 40 or ω_7 > 1000 only 275 would be charged, ω′_7 = 40 and nothing would change
ω_7 is a page count to add: pages [40, 90) become writable, g = 275 + 50·121 = 6,325 is charged and ω′_7 = 90; a request that would pass b is clamped to b rather than refused

ω_7 is an octet count as with sbrk: the heap grows by 50 octets rounded up to one whole page, ω′_7 = the previous break address 40·Z_P, and only the base cost 275 is charged since a single page is added
Memory growth is already priced by the per-basic-block gas model, so grow_heap only charges its base cost 275 regardless of the number of pages; pages [40, 50) become writable and ω′_7 = 50

stem: Service 7 (accumulating) calls `eject` (index 22) with ω_7 = 9 and ω_8 = o, where μ[o..+32] = h. Under GP 0.8.0, when does the call return OK, and what happens then?
options: Service 9's code hash equals the code hash of service 7 (same code) and its parent field a_p = 7; a_i must be 0 and its balance already below a_t; then 9 is deleted and its balance is burned

Service 9 exists, is not the caller, and its code hash equals E_32(7); its footprint is exactly a_i = 2 with l = max(81, a_o) − 81 (one request (h, l), no storage); a_l[(h, l)] = [x, y] with y < t − D; then 9 is deleted and its entire balance is added to service 7
Service 9's code hash equals E_32(7) and its only request (h, l) is still unprovided ([]), proving nobody depends on it; then 9 is deleted and its balance is credited to the registrar
Service 9's code hash equals E_32(7), a_i = 2 and a_l[(h, l)] = [x, y, w] with w < t − D (re-requested but expired again); then 9 is deleted and its balance is credited to 7

gpRef: eq. B.2, B.6, B.11 (default branch); JIP-1 (host call 100)
stem: A service executes `ecalli 100` (`log`). Which statement is correct?
options: `log` is host call 100 of GP App. B, available in all three invocations: it returns OK, costs M_∅ and, like every other host call that reads memory, panics (☇) when the message range is not readable
`log` is consensus-critical: the formatted message is hashed into the service's accumulation output (θ) and hence into the BEEFY root, so all nodes must implement byte-identical formatting

`log` is specified by JIP-1, not by the Gray Paper: its observable effects match an unimplemented index — ω′_7 = WHAT and the gas of a bad-index call — and an unreadable message/target range must have no side-effects (no panic); the node merely prints the message
`log` exists only in Ψ_R as a guarantor diagnostic and is unavailable during accumulate and is-authorized, where `ecalli 100` falls through to the WHAT default of the mutator
